title: Comprehensive Neuro Set 1: Olfaction and Gustation (Short Answer)

questions.prompt: How are olfactory receptor cells unique compared to other sensory receptors (like those for taste or hearing) in terms of their neural classification?
questions.modelAnswer: They are primary afferent neurons (true neurons) that conduct action potentials directly into the CNS, unlike other receptors which are specialized epithelial cells.

questions.prompt: What specific type of cell in the olfactory epithelium acts as a stem cell to continuously replace olfactory receptor neurons throughout adult life?
Name the specific bone structure that olfactory axons must pass through to reach the olfactory bulb, and identify the clinical condition that results if these axons are severed here.
questions.modelAnswer: The cribriform plate (of the ethmoid bone); damage results in anosmia (loss of smell).

questions.prompt: In the biochemical cascade of olfactory transduction, which specific G protein is activated, and what is the resulting second messenger?
questions.modelAnswer: The G protein is Golf; the second messenger is cyclic AMP (cAMP).

questions.prompt: Which specific ion channels are opened by increased intracellular cAMP in the olfactory receptor membrane to produce a depolarizing receptor potential?
questions.modelAnswer: Cation channels (permeable to Na^+, K^+, and Ca^(2+)).

questions.prompt: Define "glomeruli" within the context of the olfactory bulb and identify the second-order neurons that synapse there.
questions.modelAnswer: Glomeruli are clusters of synapses in the olfactory bulb where approximately 1000 olfactory receptor axons converge onto a single mitral cell (the second-order neuron).

questions.prompt: What is the primary function of granule and periglomerular cells in the olfactory bulb regarding the "sharpening" of sensory information?
questions.modelAnswer: They are inhibitory interneurons that provide lateral inhibition, sharpening the contrast between different odors.

questions.prompt: Which major olfactory tract projects to the primary olfactory cortex (prepiriform cortex) without first relaying in the thalamus?
Distinguish between the three cell types found within a taste bud: receptor cells, supporting cells, and basal cells.
questions.modelAnswer: Receptor cells are the transducers; supporting cells have an unknown function (do not respond to stimuli); basal cells are stem cell precursors.

questions.prompt: Which type of taste papillae is the largest, contains the most taste buds, and is arranged in a V-shape on the posterior tongue?
Match the three cranial nerves (VII, IX, and X) to the specific regions of the tongue or throat they innervate for the sense of taste.
questions.modelAnswer: CN VII (Facial/Chorda tympani): anterior two-thirds of the tongue. CN IX (Glossopharyngeal): posterior one-third of the tongue. CN X (Vagus): back of the throat and epiglottis.

questions.prompt: Describe the cellular mechanism by which "salty" and "sour" tastes are transduced in a taste receptor cell.
questions.modelAnswer: Salty (Na^+): Na^+enters directly through epithelial Na^+channels (ENaC). Sour (H^+): H^+enters through ENaC or blocks K^+channels, leading to depolarization.

questions.prompt: Which G protein and second messenger system are utilized for the transduction of "bitter," "sweet," and "umami" tastes?
questions.modelAnswer: The G protein gustducin; it uses the IP3/Ca^(2+)mechanism to open transient receptor potential (TRP) channels.

questions.prompt: Identify the specific thalamic relay nucleus and the brainstem nucleus (within the solitary tract) where taste information is processed en route to the cortex.
questions.modelAnswer: Brainstem: Solitary nucleus (medulla). Thalamus: Ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus.

questions.prompt: Which elementary taste quality generally has the lowest stimulation threshold, and what is the presumed evolutionary benefit of this sensitivity?
questions.modelAnswer: Bitter has the lowest threshold; it serves as a protective mechanism against many toxic substances found in nature.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the vomeronasal organ (VNO) found in many mammals?
questions.modelAnswer: It detects pheromones, which influence social and sexual behavior.
